o: We simulate two arrays: seen (positive integers, newest first) and ans. For each -1 we count consecutive -1s (resetting when a positive appears) and report the k-th element of seen, or -1 if seen is too short. Example 1 yields [2,1,-1] because the third consecutive -1 outruns the two-element seen list; example 2 shows the streak resetting after the 2. Constraints (n <= 100) make direct simulation trivially fast.
k: Track the run length of consecutive -1s and reset it on any positive number.
Prepending to seen means index k-1 in a normal list representation.

a.i: Keep seen as a list where new positives are inserted at the front (or appended and read from the back). Maintain k, the current streak of -1s. On a positive, reset k to 0 and record the value; on -1, increment k and answer from seen if possible.
s: For each num: if positive, insert at front of seen and set k = 0.
If -1, increment k; append seen[k-1] to ans if k <= len(seen) else append -1.
a.t: O(n^2) worst case due to front insertion, trivial for n <= 100.

a.i: Instead of inserting at the front (O(n) per op), append positives to the end and treat the last k appended positives as the answer source: the k-th most recent positive is seen[len(seen)-k]. Same results, O(1) per insertion.
s: Append positives to seen instead of prepending.
On -1 with streak k, access seen[len(seen)-k] when k <= len(seen).
a.t: O(n) time — each element processed once with O(1) operations.

w: Either approach passes easily; prefer the append variant to show awareness of insertion costs. Edge cases: -1 as the very first element (answer -1), and streaks longer than the number of positives seen so far.
